title: Kinematics: Equations of Uniformly Accelerated Motion (NCERT Class 11)
answer: For an object moving in a straight line with constant acceleration a, the three fundamental kinematic equations of motion are: 1) v = u + at, 2) s = ut + ½at², and 3) v² = u² + 2as (where u is initial velocity, v is final velocity, s is displacement, and t is time).
highlights: First Equation (Velocity-Time): v = u + at
Second Equation (Position-Time): s = ut + ½at²
Third Equation (Position-Velocity): v² = u² + 2as
Displacement in nth second: s_n = u + ½a(2n - 1)

title: Work-Energy Theorem & Conservation of Energy (NCERT Class 11)
answer: The Work-Energy Theorem states that the net work done by all forces acting on a body equals the change in its kinetic energy: W_net = ΔK = ½mv² - ½mu². In a conservative force field, total mechanical energy (Kinetic + Potential) remains constant.
highlights: Work Done Formula: W = F · d = F · d · cos(θ) (in Joules)
Work-Energy Theorem: W_net = K_final - K_initial = ½m(v² - u²)
Potential Energy: Gravitational PE = mgh; Elastic Spring PE = ½kx²
Power: Instantaneous Power P = dW/dt = F · v (measured in Watts, W)

title: Rotational Motion, Torque & Moment of Inertia (NCERT Class 11)
answer: Moment of Inertia (I = Σ m_i·r_i²) is the rotational analogue of mass, measuring an object's resistance to rotational acceleration. Torque is the rotational analogue of force (τ = I·α = r × F), and angular momentum (L = I·ω) is conserved in the absence of external torque.
highlights: Torque: τ = r × F = rF sin(θ) = I·α (in N·m)
Angular Momentum: L = r × p = I·ω (Conservation: If τ_ext = 0, then I₁ω₁ = I₂ω₂)
Rotational Kinetic Energy: K_rot = ½Iω²
Theorems of Moment of Inertia: Parallel Axes Theorem (I = I_cm + Md²) and Perpendicular Axes Theorem (I_z = I_x + I_y for planar lamina)

keywords: law of periods t2 proportional to r3
title: Kepler's Three Laws of Planetary Motion (NCERT Class 11)
answer: Johannes Kepler formulated three empirical laws of planetary motion: 1) Law of Orbits (All planets move in elliptical orbits with the Sun at one focus); 2) Law of Areas (A line segment joining a planet and the Sun sweeps out equal areas in equal intervals of time, confirming conservation of angular momentum); 3) Law of Periods (The square of orbital period T is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis a: T² ∝ a³).
highlights: 1st Law (Elliptical Orbits): Planet orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one of the two foci
2nd Law (Equal Areas): Areal velocity dA/dt = L / (2m) = Constant (Planet moves fastest at perihelion and slowest at aphelion)
3rd Law (Harmonic Law): T² / a³ = (4π²) / (G·M_sun) = Constant
Newton's Synthesis: Isaac Newton used Kepler's third law to deduce the inverse-square law of Universal Gravitation (F = G·m₁m₂/r²)

title: Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) & Simple Pendulum (NCERT Class 11)
answer: Simple Harmonic Motion (SHM) is a periodic oscillatory motion where the restoring force is directly proportional to displacement from the mean position and acts in the opposite direction: F = -kx (or a = -ω²x). The time period of a simple pendulum of length l is T = 2π√(l / g).
highlights: Differential Equation: d²x/dt² + ω²x = 0 (Displacement x(t) = A·sin(ωt + φ))
Velocity in SHM: v(x) = ±ω√(A² - x²) (Maximum velocity v_max = Aω at mean position x = 0)
Total Energy in SHM: E = K + U = ½mω²A² = Constant at all points of oscillation
Simple Pendulum: T = 2π√(l / g) (independent of the mass of the bob and depends only on length and gravity)

keywords: first and second law of thermodynamics
title: Carnot Engine & Thermodynamic Efficiency (NCERT Class 11)
answer: A Carnot engine is an idealized reversible heat engine operating between two temperatures (source at T₁ and sink at T₂). Its maximum theoretical thermal efficiency is given by η = 1 - (T₂ / T₁) = 1 - (Q₂ / Q₁), proving that no engine can be 100% efficient without a sink at absolute zero.
highlights: Carnot Efficiency Formula: η = 1 - (T_sink / T_source) = (T₁ - T₂) / T₁ (Temperatures in Kelvin)
Four Reversible Steps of Carnot Cycle: 1) Isothermal expansion at T₁, 2) Adiabatic expansion from T₁ to T₂, 3) Isothermal compression at T₂, 4) Adiabatic compression from T₂ to T₁
Carnot's Theorem: No real heat engine operating between two given heat reservoirs can be more efficient than a reversible Carnot engine operating between the same reservoirs

keywords: electric field of point charge class 12
title: Coulomb's Law & Gauss's Law in Electrostatics (NCERT Class 12)
answer: Coulomb's Law states that electrostatic force between two stationary point charges is F = (1 / 4πε₀) · (|q₁q₂| / r²). Gauss's Law states that the total electric flux through any closed Gaussian surface equals the enclosed net electric charge divided by the permittivity of free space: Φ_E = ∮ E · dA = Q_enclosed / ε₀.
highlights: Coulomb's Constant: k = 1 / (4πε₀) ≈ 8.98755 × 10⁹ N·m²/C²
Permittivity of Free Space: ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C²·N⁻¹·m⁻²
Gauss's Law Equation: Φ_E = ∮ E · dA = Q_enclosed / ε₀
Applications of Gauss's Law: Electric field due to infinite line charge (E = λ / 2πε₀r), infinite planar sheet (E = σ / 2ε₀), and spherical charged shell

title: Kirchhoff's Circuit Laws & Wheatstone Bridge (NCERT Class 12)
answer: Kirchhoff's First Law (Current Law / KCL / Junction Rule) states that the algebraic sum of currents entering a junction is zero (Σ I = 0, based on conservation of charge). Kirchhoff's Second Law (Voltage Law / KVL / Loop Rule) states that the sum of all potential differences around any closed circuit loop is zero (Σ ΔV = 0, based on conservation of energy).
highlights: Kirchhoff's Current Law (KCL): Σ I_in = Σ I_out (Conservation of Electric Charge)
Kirchhoff's Voltage Law (KVL): Σ V + Σ (IR) = 0 around any closed loop (Conservation of Energy)
Wheatstone Bridge Principle: When bridge is balanced (galvanometer deflection = 0), ratio of resistances is P / Q = R / S
Metre Bridge: Practical laboratory application of balanced Wheatstone bridge to measure unknown resistance

title: Faraday's and Lenz's Laws of Electromagnetic Induction
answer: Faraday's Law states that the magnitude of induced electromotive force (EMF) is proportional to the time rate of change of magnetic flux: ε = -dΦ_B/dt. Lenz's Law (represented by the negative sign) states that the induced current always flows in such a direction as to oppose the change in flux producing it (consequence of conservation of energy).
highlights: Magnetic Flux: Φ_B = B · A · cosθ (measured in Webers; 1 Wb = 1 T·m²)
Induced EMF in a rotating coil: ε = NBAω sin(ωt) (foundation of AC generators)
Self-inductance (L): Induced EMF ε = -L(dI/dt) (measured in Henrys)
Mutual inductance (M): ε₂ = -M(dI₁/dt) (foundation of electrical transformers)

title: Einstein's Photoelectric Effect & Equation
answer: Einstein's Photoelectric Equation: K_max = hν - Φ₀ = hc/λ - hν₀, where hν is photon energy, Φ₀ = hν₀ is the work function of the metal, and K_max is the maximum kinetic energy of emitted photoelectrons. Albert Einstein won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for explaining this phenomenon.
highlights: Emission occurs instantaneously (< 10⁻⁹ s) if light frequency ν ≥ threshold frequency ν₀
Number of photoelectrons emitted per second is directly proportional to light INTENSITY
Maximum kinetic energy depends strictly on light FREQUENCY, completely independent of intensity
Provides definitive experimental proof of the particle/photon nature of light (E = hν, where h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s)

title: Bohr's Model of the Hydrogen Atom (NCERT Class 12)
answer: Niels Bohr's atomic model (1913) postulates that electrons revolve around the nucleus only in non-radiating stable orbits with quantized angular momentum (L = mvr = nh / 2π). The energy of an electron in the nth orbit of hydrogen is E_n = -13.6 / n² eV.
highlights: Angular Momentum Quantization: L = mvr = n·(h / 2π) (where n = 1, 2, 3... is principal quantum number)
Radius of nth Orbit: r_n = n²·a₀ = 0.529 × n² Å (Bohr radius a₀ = 0.529 Å)
Energy Levels: E_n = -13.6 / n² eV (Ground state E₁ = -13.6 eV; Ionization energy = +13.6 eV)
Hydrogen Spectral Series: Lyman (UV: n₁=1), Balmer (Visible: n₁=2), Paschen (Infrared: n₁=3), Brackett (IR: n₁=4), Pfund (Far-IR: n₁=5)

title: Quantum Numbers, Aufbau Principle & Electronic Configuration (NCERT Class 11)
answer: Four quantum numbers uniquely specify the state of an electron in an atom: Principal (n), Azimuthal/Orbital (l = 0 to n-1), Magnetic (m_l = -l to +l), and Spin (m_s = ±½). Electrons fill atomic orbitals in order of increasing energy according to the Aufbau (n + l) rule.
highlights: Four Quantum Numbers: 1) n (Shell size & energy: 1,2,3...), 2) l (Subshell shape: s=0, p=1, d=2, f=3), 3) m_l (Orbital spatial orientation: 2l+1 values), 4) m_s (Electron spin: +½, -½)
Aufbau Principle: Orbitals with lower (n + l) value are filled first; if (n + l) is identical, the orbital with lower n fills first
Pauli Exclusion Principle: No two electrons in an atom can have identical values for all four quantum numbers (max 2 electrons per orbital with opposite spins)
Hund's Rule: Pairing of electrons in degenerate orbitals (p, d, f) does not occur until each orbital is singly occupied with parallel spins

title: Chemical Bonding: VSEPR, Hybridization & Molecular Orbital Theory (NCERT Class 11)
answer: VSEPR theory predicts molecular geometries by minimizing electrostatic repulsion between valence shell electron pairs (Lone pair-Lone pair > Lone pair-Bond pair > Bond pair-Bond pair). Molecular Orbital Theory (MOT) calculates bond order as: Bond Order = ½(N_b - N_a), where N_b and N_a are electrons in bonding and antibonding orbitals.
highlights: Hybridization & Shapes: sp (Linear, 180°, BeCl₂/C₂H₂), sp² (Trigonal planar, 120°, BF₃/C₂H₄), sp³ (Tetrahedral, 109.5°, CH₄), sp³d (Trigonal bipyramidal, PCl₅), sp³d² (Octahedral, SF₆)
Repulsion Hierarchy: Lone Pair–Lone Pair > Lone Pair–Bond Pair > Bond Pair–Bond Pair (e.g., NH₃ is pyramidal 107°, H₂O is bent 104.5° due to lone pair repulsion)
Bond Order (MOT): Bond Order = ½(N_b - N_a) (Higher bond order = greater stability and shorter bond length; O₂ has bond order 2 and is paramagnetic due to 2 unpaired electrons in π*2p orbitals)

title: Chemical Equilibrium & Le Chatelier's Principle (NCERT Class 11)
answer: Le Chatelier's Principle states that if a dynamic equilibrium system is subjected to a change in concentration, temperature, or pressure, the equilibrium will shift in the direction that counteracts and relieves the applied change.
highlights: Concentration Effect: Increasing reactant concentration shifts equilibrium in forward direction (towards products)
Pressure Effect: Increasing pressure shifts equilibrium towards the side with fewer moles of gaseous molecules (e.g., Haber's N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ shifts forward under high pressure)
Temperature Effect: Increasing temperature favors endothermic reactions (ΔH > 0); decreasing temperature favors exothermic reactions (ΔH < 0)
Relation between K_p and K_c: K_p = K_c · (RT)^(Δn_g) (where Δn_g = moles of gaseous products - moles of gaseous reactants)

title: Electrochemistry: Nernst Equation & Kohlrausch's Law (NCERT Class 12)
answer: The Nernst equation relates the cell potential of an electrochemical cell to standard electrode potential and reaction quotient Q at 298 K: E_cell = E°_cell - (0.0591 / n) · log₁₀(Q). Kohlrausch's Law states that the limiting molar conductivity of an electrolyte is the sum of the individual limiting ionic conductivities of its cations and anions.
highlights: Nernst Equation at 298 K: E_cell = E°_cell - (0.0591 / n) · log₁₀([Anode] / [Cathode])
Standard Gibbs Free Energy: ΔG° = -nFE°_cell = -RT ln(K_c)
Kohlrausch's Law of Independent Migration: Λ°_m(NaCl) = λ°(Na⁺) + λ°(Cl⁻) (enables determination of Λ°_m for weak electrolytes like CH₃COOH)
Faraday's Laws of Electrolysis: 1st Law: Mass deposited m = Z·I·t (Z is electrochemical equivalent); 2nd Law: m ∝ Equivalent weight for identical current

keywords: rate of reaction order and molecularity
title: Chemical Kinetics, Reaction Order & Arrhenius Equation (NCERT Class 12)
answer: Chemical kinetics investigates reaction rates, mechanisms, and activation energy. For a first-order reaction, the integrated rate equation is k = (2.303 / t) · log₁₀([R]₀ / [R]), with a half-life t_½ = 0.693 / k independent of initial concentration. The Arrhenius Equation governs temperature dependence: k = A·e^(-E_a / RT).
highlights: First-Order Integrated Rate Law: k = (2.303 / t) · log₁₀([A]₀ / [A])
Half-Life Formulas: Zero order: t_½ = [A]₀ / 2k; First order: t_½ = 0.693 / k (independent of initial concentration)
Arrhenius Equation: ln(k₂ / k₁) = (E_a / R) · [(1 / T₁) - (1 / T₂)]

Order vs Molecularity: Order is experimentally determined and can be fractional/zero; Molecularity is a theoretical count of colliding reactant species in an elementary step and is always a non-zero positive integer (1, 2, 3)

title: Nucleophilic Substitution Mechanisms: SN1 vs SN2 (NCERT Class 12)
answer: SN1 (Unimolecular Nucleophilic Substitution) is a two-step mechanism proceeding via a planar carbocation intermediate yielding racemic products (reactivity: 3° > 2° > 1° alkyl halides, favored by polar protic solvents). SN2 (Bimolecular) is a concerted single-step backside attack with a pentacoordinated transition state resulting in 100% Walden inversion of configuration (reactivity: 1° > 2° > 3°, favored by polar aprotic solvents).
highlights: SN1 Mechanism: Rate = k[Alkyl Halide] (Two steps: slow carbocation formation followed by fast nucleophile attack; tertiary alkyl halides most reactive due to 3° carbocation stability)
SN2 Mechanism: Rate = k[Alkyl Halide][Nucleophile] (Single-step backside attack causing complete Walden inversion; methyl & primary halides most reactive due to low steric hindrance)
Stereochemistry: SN1 leads to racemization (d + l mixture); SN2 leads to complete stereochemical inversion

title: Aldol Condensation & Cannizzaro Reaction (NCERT Class 12)
answer: Aldol condensation occurs when aldehydes or ketones possessing at least one α-hydrogen react with dilute alkali (NaOH) to form β-hydroxy aldehydes (aldols), which upon heating lose water to yield α,β-unsaturated carbonyls. The Cannizzaro reaction occurs in aldehydes lacking α-hydrogen (e.g., formaldehyde, benzaldehyde) with concentrated alkali, undergoing self-redox (disproportionation) into an alcohol and a carboxylate salt.
highlights: Aldol Condensation: Requires α-hydrogen; 2 CH₃CHO + dil. NaOH → CH₃-CH(OH)-CH₂-CHO (Aldol) → CH₃-CH=CH-CHO (Crotonaldehyde + H₂O)
Cannizzaro Reaction: Lacks α-hydrogen; 2 HCHO + 50% conc. NaOH → CH₃OH (Methanol) + HCOONa (Sodium Formate)
Cross-Aldol Condensation: Carried out between two different carbonyl compounds yielding a mixture of four distinct condensation products

title: Permutations (nPr) & Combinations (nCr) (NCERT Class 11)
answer: Permutation represents ordered arrangements of r items chosen from n distinct items: nPr = n! / (n - r)!. Combination represents unordered selections of r items from n distinct items: nCr = n! / [r! · (n - r)!].
highlights: Permutation (Order matters): nPr = n! / (n - r)! (e.g., arranging letters in words, seating arrangements)
Combination (Order does not matter): nCr = n! / [r!(n - r)!] = nPr / r! (e.g., forming committees, selecting teams)
Symmetry Property: nCr = nC(n - r)
Pascal's Identity: nCr + nC(r - 1) = (n + 1)Cr

title: Binomial Theorem for Positive Integral Index (NCERT Class 11)
answer: The Binomial Theorem expands any positive integer power of a binomial (a + b)ⁿ as: (a + b)ⁿ = Σₖ₌₀ⁿ [ⁿCₖ · aⁿ⁻ᵏ · bᵏ] = ⁿC₀·aⁿ + ⁿC₁·aⁿ⁻¹b + ... + ⁿCₙ·bⁿ. The expansion contains exactly (n + 1) terms.
highlights: Standard Formula: (a + b)ⁿ = ⁿC₀ aⁿ + ⁿC₁ aⁿ⁻¹b + ⁿC₂ aⁿ⁻²b² + ... + ⁿCₙ bⁿ
General Term: T_(r+1) = ⁿC_r · aⁿ⁻ʳ · bʳ
Middle Term: If n is even, one middle term at T_((n/2)+1); If n is odd, two middle terms at T_((n+1)/2) and T_((n+3)/2)
Sum of Binomial Coefficients: ⁿC₀ + ⁿC₁ + ⁿC₂ + ... + ⁿCₙ = 2ⁿ

title: Matrices, Determinants & Inverse Matrix (NCERT Class 12)
answer: The inverse of a square non-singular matrix A (where |A| ≠ 0) is calculated as A⁻¹ = (1 / |A|) · adj(A), satisfying A · A⁻¹ = A⁻¹ · A = I. A matrix is singular if its determinant is zero (|A| = 0), in which case its inverse does not exist.
highlights: Matrix Inverse Formula: A⁻¹ = adj(A) / |A| (where adj(A) is the transpose of the matrix of cofactors)
Inversion Properties: (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹; (A^T)⁻¹ = (A⁻¹)^T; |A⁻¹| = 1 / |A|
Determinant Properties: |AB| = |A|·|B|; |kA| = kⁿ|A| for an n×n square matrix; |adj(A)| = |A|ⁿ⁻¹
Solving Systems of Linear Equations: Matrix Method X = A⁻¹B

title: Bayes' Theorem & Conditional Probability (NCERT Class 12)
answer: Bayes' Theorem calculates the posterior probability of an event E_i given that an outcome A has occurred: P(E_i | A) = [P(E_i) · P(A | E_i)] / [Σⱼ P(E_j) · P(A | E_j)]. Conditional probability is defined as P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B).
highlights: Bayes' Formula: P(E_i | A) = [P(E_i) · P(A | E_i)] / [Σₖ P(E_k) · P(A | E_k)]
Conditional Probability: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B) (where P(B) > 0)
Independent Events: Two events A and B are independent if and only if P(A ∩ B) = P(A) · P(B)
Applications: Medical diagnostic test evaluation (false positive/negative rates), machine learning spam classification

title: Cell Cycle & Cell Division: Mitosis vs Meiosis (NCERT Class 11)
answer: Mitosis is equational cell division in somatic cells yielding 2 genetically identical diploid (2n) daughter cells through Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, and Telophase. Meiosis is reductional division in germ cells producing 4 genetically varied haploid (n) gametes via two successive nuclear divisions (Meiosis I and Meiosis II), with genetic crossing-over occurring during Pachytene of Prophase I.
highlights: Mitosis (Equational): 1 cell division → 2 identical diploid (2n) daughter cells (responsible for growth and tissue repair)
Meiosis (Reductional): 2 cell divisions → 4 genetically unique haploid (n) daughter cells (produces sperm and egg gametes)

Meiosis I Prophase I Sub-stages: Leptotene → Zygotene (Synapsis / Synaptonemal complex) → Pachytene (Crossing Over mediated by recombinase enzyme) → Diplotene (Chiasmata formation) → Diakinesis (Terminalization)
Anaphase Distinction: In Mitosis Anaphase, sister chromatids split; In Meiosis Anaphase I, homologous chromosome pairs separate while sister chromatids remain attached

monohybrid and dihybrid cross ratio class 12
title: Mendelian Genetics & Laws of Inheritance (NCERT Class 12)
answer: Gregor Johann Mendel established classical genetics through experiments on garden peas (Pisum sativum), formulating three fundamental laws: 1) Law of Dominance, 2) Law of Segregation (purity of gametes: alleles separate during gametogenesis), and 3) Law of Independent Assortment (genes for different traits sort independently).
highlights: Monohybrid Cross (One trait): Phenotypic ratio = 3:1 (Tall:Dwarf); Genotypic ratio = 1:2:1 (TT:Tt:tt)
Dihybrid Cross (Two traits): Phenotypic ratio = 9:3:3:1 (Round Yellow : Round Green : Wrinkled Yellow : Wrinkled Green)
Law of Segregation: The two alleles of a gene separate during meiosis so that each gamete carries only one allele
Exceptions to Mendelism: Incomplete dominance (Mirabilis jalapa 1:2:1 pink flowers), Co-dominance (ABO blood groups / AB allele expression), Pleiotropy, Polygenic inheritance

title: Central Dogma: DNA Replication, Transcription & Translation (NCERT Class 12)
answer: The Central Dogma of Molecular Biology (proposed by Francis Crick) states the directional flow of genetic information: DNA → (Transcription) → mRNA → (Translation) → Protein. DNA replication is semi-conservative (proved by Meselson and Stahl in 1958 using ¹⁵N isotope in E. coli).
highlights: DNA Replication: Semi-conservative and semi-discontinuous; DNA Polymerase synthesizes 5'→3' (Leading strand continuous, Lagging strand produces Okazaki fragments joined by DNA ligase)
Transcription: Synthesis of RNA from DNA template by RNA Polymerase (Promoter → Structural gene → Terminator)
Genetic Code: 64 triplet codons (61 code for 20 amino acids, 3 Stop codons: UAA, UAG, UGA; Start codon AUG codes for Methionine); Universal, Degenerate, Unambiguous, and Non-overlapping
Translation: Protein synthesis at ribosomes where tRNA anticodons read mRNA codons to assemble polypeptide chains

title: Biotechnology: Recombinant DNA & PCR (NCERT Class 12)
answer: Recombinant DNA (rDNA) technology constructs hybrid DNA using restriction endonucleases ('molecular scissors' that cut at specific palindromic recognition sequences) and DNA ligase. The Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR), invented by Kary Mullis in 1983, amplifies a specific DNA segment billion-fold in vitro in three thermal cycles: Denaturation (94°C), Annealing (54°C), and Extension (72°C using thermostable Taq polymerase).
highlights: Three PCR Steps: 1) Denaturation (~94°C — separates double strands), 2) Annealing (~50–60°C — primers bind), 3) Extension (72°C — Taq DNA polymerase from thermophilic bacterium Thermus aquaticus synthesizes complementary strands)
Restriction Enzymes: Cut DNA at palindromic sequences generating sticky or blunt ends (e.g., EcoRI cuts at 5'-GAATTC-3')
Gel Electrophoresis: Separates negatively charged DNA fragments by size towards the positive anode in an agarose gel matrix, visualized under UV light with Ethidium Bromide (EtBr)
Cloning Vectors: Plasmids (e.g., pBR322 with ori, amp^R, tet^R selectable markers) and bacteriophages

title: Human Endocrine System & Major Hormones (NCERT Class 11)
answer: The endocrine system consists of ductless glands that secrete chemical messenger hormones directly into the bloodstream. The Pituitary Gland is the 'Master Gland' controlled by the Hypothalamus, the Thyroid produces Thyroxine (regulating basal metabolic rate), the Pancreas secretes Insulin and Glucagon (regulating blood glucose), and the Adrenals release Adrenaline ('fight-or-flight' hormone).
highlights: Hypothalamus & Pituitary: Hypothalamus secretes releasing/inhibiting hormones; Pituitary secretes GH (Growth Hormone), TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH, Prolactin, Oxytocin, and ADH/Vasopressin
Thyroid Gland: Secretes Thyroxine (T₄) and Triiodothyronine (T₃) containing iodine; deficiency causes Goitre (swelling of neck)
Pancreas (Islets of Langerhans): β-cells secrete Insulin (lowers blood sugar); α-cells secrete Glucagon (raises blood sugar); insulin deficiency causes Diabetes Mellitus
Adrenal Glands: Adrenal medulla secretes Adrenaline (Epinephrine) and Noradrenaline for emergency stress responses (increases heart rate, respiration, alertness)

title: Microeconomics: Price Elasticity of Demand (NCERT Class 12)
answer: Price Elasticity of Demand (E_d) measures the percentage responsiveness of the quantity demanded of a good to a change in its price: E_d = (% Change in Quantity Demanded) / (% Change in Price) = (ΔQ / ΔP) · (P / Q).
highlights: Elasticity Degrees: Perfectly Inelastic (E_d = 0, vertical demand curve), Inelastic (0 < E_d < 1, necessities like medicines/salt), Unitary Elastic (E_d = 1, rectangular hyperbola), Elastic (E_d > 1, luxury goods), Perfectly Elastic (E_d = ∞, horizontal line)
Determinants: Availability of close substitutes, nature of the good (necessity vs luxury), proportion of consumer income spent, and time horizon
Total Outlay Method: If price and total expenditure move in opposite directions, E_d > 1; if they move in same direction, E_d < 1; if expenditure remains constant, E_d = 1

title: Macroeconomics: National Income Accounting (GDP, GNP, NNP) (NCERT Class 12)
answer: Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is the total monetary value of all final goods and services produced within the domestic geographic boundary of a country during a financial year. National Income is formally defined as Net National Product at Factor Cost (NNP_FC = GNP - Depreciation - Net Indirect Taxes).
highlights: GDP Formula (Expenditure Method): GDP = C + I + G + (X - M) [Consumption + Investment + Government Spending + Net Exports]
GNP: GDP + NFIA (Net Factor Income from Abroad)
NNP at Market Price: GNP - Depreciation (Consumption of Fixed Capital)
National Income (NNP_FC): NNP_MP - Net Indirect Taxes (Indirect Taxes - Subsidies)
Real vs Nominal GDP: Real GDP is evaluated at constant base-year prices (adjusted for inflation); Nominal GDP is evaluated at current market prices

title: Coulomb's Law of Electrostatics
answer: Coulomb's Law states that the electrostatic force (F) between two point charges q₁ and q₂ separated by distance r is F = (1 / 4πε₀) · (|q₁q₂| / r²), where ε₀ = 8.854 × 10⁻¹² C²/(N·m²) and 1/(4πε₀) ≈ 8.988 × 10⁹ N·m²/C².
highlights: Inverse square law: Force is directly proportional to product of charges and inversely proportional to r²
Vector form: F₁₂ = -F₂₁ (obeys Newton's Third Law)
Dielectric medium of constant K reduces force by factor K: F_med = F_vac / K
Valid strictly for static point charges in vacuum or uniform dielectric

answer: Gauss's Law states that the total electric flux (Φ_E) through any closed Gaussian surface equals the net charge enclosed (q_enc) divided by the permittivity of free space: ∮ E · dA = q_enc / ε₀.

Electric field due to infinite line charge: E = λ / (2πε₀r)
Electric field due to infinite plane sheet of charge: E = σ / (2ε₀) (independent of distance)
Electric field inside a uniformly charged conducting sphere or hollow shell is ZERO (E = 0)

title: Bohr's Model of the Hydrogen Atom (1913)
answer: Niels Bohr postulated that electrons revolve in non-radiating discrete circular orbits where orbital angular momentum is quantized: L = mvr = nh / 2π (n = 1, 2, 3...). Energy of electron in nth orbit: E_n = -13.6 / n² eV. Radius of nth orbit: r_n = 0.529 · n² / Z Å.
highlights: Bohr radius for hydrogen (n=1, Z=1): a₀ = 0.529 Å (0.0529 nm)
Ground state energy of hydrogen: E₁ = -13.6 eV; Ionization energy = +13.6 eV
Hydrogen Spectral Series: Lyman (UV, n₁=1), Balmer (Visible, n₁=2), Paschen (IR, n₁=3), Brackett (IR, n₁=4), Pfund (IR, n₁=5)
Rydberg formula: 1/λ = R_H · Z² · (1/n₁² - 1/n₂²), where R_H ≈ 1.097 × 10⁷ m⁻¹

title: Semiconductor Devices — P-N Junctions and Transistors
answer: A P-N junction diode forms a depletion region with a barrier potential (~0.7 V for Si, ~0.3 V for Ge). Forward bias reduces the barrier allowing high current; reverse bias widens the barrier, blocking current (used for rectification). A BJT (Bipolar Junction Transistor) has Emitter, Base, and Collector terminals functioning as an amplifier or electronic switch.
highlights: Forward bias: P to positive terminal, N to negative — conducts with exponential current rise
Reverse bias: P to negative, N to positive — only tiny microampere leakage current flows until Zener breakdown
Zener diode: Operates in reverse breakdown as a precise voltage regulator
Half-wave rectifier efficiency = 40.6%; Full-wave center-tapped/bridge rectifier efficiency = 81.2%

title: Chemical Equilibrium and Le Chatelier's Principle
answer: Chemical equilibrium is a dynamic state where the rate of forward reaction equals the rate of reverse reaction. Le Chatelier's Principle states that if a dynamic equilibrium is disturbed by changing temperature, pressure, or concentration, the system adjusts to counteract the change.
highlights: Equilibrium constant relation: K_p = K_c · (RT)^(Δn_g), where Δn_g = moles of gaseous products - moles of gaseous reactants
Haber Process for Ammonia: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) + 92.4 kJ (exothermic; favored by high pressure ~200 atm and moderate temp ~450°C with Fe catalyst)
Catalyst accelerates rate of both forward and backward reactions equally without shifting equilibrium position K_eq
Adding inert gas at constant volume has NO effect on equilibrium

title: Electrochemistry — Nernst Equation and Galvanic Cells
answer: The Nernst Equation calculates cell potential under non-standard conditions: E_cell = E°_cell - (2.303 RT / nF) · log₁₀(Q). At 298 K (25°C): E_cell = E°_cell - (0.0591 / n) · log₁₀(Q). Standard hydrogen electrode (SHE) is assigned E° = 0.00 V as universal reference.
highlights: Galvanic cell converts chemical energy to electrical energy: Anode is negative (Oxidation), Cathode is positive (Reduction) [AnOx - RedCat]
Gibbs Free Energy relation: ΔG° = -nFE°_cell = -2.303 RT log₁₀(K_eq)
Faraday's First Law: Mass deposited m = Z · I · t, where Z is electrochemical equivalent (Z = M / (nF))
1 Faraday (F) = 96,485 Coulombs (charge on 1 mole of electrons)

title: Chemical Kinetics — Rate Laws and Arrhenius Equation
answer: Chemical kinetics studies reaction rates and mechanisms. For a First Order reaction: Rate = k[A]¹, integrated rate law k = (2.303/t) · log₁₀([A]₀/[A]), and half-life t₁/₂ = 0.693 / k (independent of initial concentration). Arrhenius Equation: k = A · e^(-E_a / RT).
highlights: Zero order: Rate = k; t₁/₂ = [A]₀ / (2k) (half-life directly proportional to initial concentration)
First order: Half-life t₁/₂ = ln(2)/k ≈ 0.693/k (constant, used in radioactive decay)
Arrhenius equation linear form: ln(k₂/k₁) = (E_a / R) · (1/T₁ - 1/T₂)
Pseudo-first-order: High excess of one reactant makes second-order reaction behave as first-order (e.g. acid hydrolysis of ester)

title: Coordination Compounds and Crystal Field Theory
answer: Coordination compounds consist of a central transition metal atom or ion bonded to surrounding electron-donating ligands via coordinate covalent bonds. Crystal Field Theory (CFT) explains colour and magnetism via d-orbital splitting in octahedral (t₂g and e_g) and tetrahedral geometries.
highlights: Werner's Theory (1893): Primary valency is ionizable (oxidation state); Secondary valency is non-ionizable (coordination number)
Octahedral splitting: Five d-orbitals split into lower energy triplet t₂g (d_xy, d_yz, d_zx) and higher energy doublet e_g (d_x²-y², d_z²)
Spectrochemical series (increasing ligand field strength): I⁻ < Br⁻ < Cl⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < H₂O < NH₃ < en < CN⁻ < CO
Strong field ligands (CN⁻, CO) cause pairing of electrons (low spin complexes); weak field ligands form high spin complexes

title: Key Named Reactions in Organic Chemistry
answer: Crucial organic named reactions include: (1) Aldol Condensation (aldehydes/ketones with α-hydrogen in dilute base form β-hydroxy aldehydes), (2) Cannizzaro Reaction (aldehydes without α-hydrogen in conc. base undergo disproportionation), (3) Reimer-Tiemann Reaction (phenol + CHCl3 + aq NaOH yields salicylaldehyde), (4) Kolbe Reaction (phenol + CO2 + NaOH yields salicylic acid).
highlights: Wurtz Reaction: 2R-X + 2Na (in dry ether) → R-R + 2NaX (synthesizes symmetrical higher alkanes)
Clemmensen Reduction: Carbonyl (C=O) + Zn-Hg/conc. HCl → CH₂ (methylene group)
Wolff-Kishner Reduction: Carbonyl + Hydrazine (NH₂NH₂) + KOH/ethylene glycol → CH₂
Friedel-Crafts Alkylation/Acylation: Benzene + R-X (with anhydrous AlCl₃ catalyst) → Alkylbenzene / Acylbenzene

keywords: watson and crick dna double helix
title: DNA Double Helix, Chargaff's Rule & Replication
answer: James Watson and Francis Crick (1953) elucidated the DNA double helix based on Rosalind Franklin's X-ray diffraction. Chargaff's Rules state: [A] = [T] and [G] = [C] with purines = pyrimidines. DNA replicates semi-conservatively (demonstrated by Meselson and Stahl in 1958 using ¹⁵N isotope).
highlights: Double helix has right-handed antiparallel strands (5'→3' and 3'→5') with pitch = 3.4 nm and 10 bp per turn
Adenine pairs with Thymine via 2 hydrogen bonds (A=T); Guanine pairs with Cytosine via 3 hydrogen bonds (G≡C)
Central Dogma (Crick): DNA → (Transcription) → mRNA → (Translation) → Protein; Reverse transcription occurs in retroviruses
Key replication enzymes: Helicase (unwinds DNA), Primase (RNA primer), DNA Polymerase III (synthesizes 5'→3'), Ligase (joins Okazaki fragments)

title: Biotechnology — Recombinant DNA and PCR
answer: Recombinant DNA technology uses Restriction Endonucleases ("molecular scissors" discovering palindromic recognition sequences) and DNA ligase to insert foreign genes into cloning vectors (e.g. pBR322). Polymerase Chain Reaction (PCR, invented by Kary Mullis in 1983) amplifies DNA billions of times using Taq polymerase across 3 steps: Denaturation (94°C), Annealing (~54°C), and Extension (72°C).
highlights: Restriction endonucleases cut specific palindromic sequences (e.g. EcoRI cuts 5'-GAATTC-3') producing sticky ends
Agarose gel electrophoresis separates DNA fragments by size toward positive anode (DNA is negatively charged)
PCR cycles: Denaturation (strands separate at 94°C) → Annealing (primers bind at ~55°C) → Extension (Taq polymerase from Thermus aquaticus extends at 72°C)
Applications: Bt cotton (pest resistance via cry genes), recombinant human insulin (Humulin by Eli Lilly in 1983), Gene therapy for ADA deficiency (1990)

title: Human Reproduction and Menstrual Cycle Hormones
answer: Human reproduction is viviparous and sexual. Spermatogenesis in testes seminiferous tubules produces 4 viable spermatozoa from 1 spermatogonium. Oogenesis produces 1 ovum and 2-3 polar bodies. The 28-day menstrual cycle is regulated by GnRH, FSH, LH, Estrogen, and Progesterone; LH surge on day 14 triggers ovulation.
highlights: Follicular phase (days 1-13): FSH stimulates follicle growth; Estrogen thickens endometrium
Ovulatory phase (day 14): Rapid LH surge causes rupture of Graafian follicle and release of secondary oocyte
Luteal phase (days 15-28): Corpus luteum secretes high Progesterone to maintain uterine lining for pregnancy
Fertilization occurs in the Ampullary-isthmic junction of Fallopian tube; Blastocyst implants in endometrium ~7 days post-fertilization

keywords: rolles theorem mean value theorem lmvt
title: Continuity, Differentiability, and Mean Value Theorems
answer: A function f(x) is continuous at x=c if lim(x→c) f(x) = f(c). Differentiability implies continuity (converse is not true, e.g. f(x)=|x| is continuous but not differentiable at x=0). Rolle's Theorem states if f is continuous on [a,b], differentiable on (a,b), and f(a)=f(b), then ∃ c ∈ (a,b) where f'(c) = 0. Lagrange's Mean Value Theorem (LMVT): f'(c) = [f(b) - f(a)] / (b - a).
highlights: Differentiability test: Left-hand derivative (LHD) must equal Right-hand derivative (RHD)
LMVT: Geometrically means tangent at some point c is parallel to the secant joining (a,f(a)) and (b,f(b))
Indeterminate forms: 0/0, ∞/∞, 0·∞, ∞-∞, 0⁰, ∞⁰, 1^∞ — evaluated using L'Hôpital's Rule: lim f(x)/g(x) = lim f'(x)/g'(x)
Intermediate Value Theorem: Continuous function on [a,b] takes every value between f(a) and f(b)

keywords: dot product cross product vector algebra
title: Vector Algebra and Three-Dimensional (3D) Geometry
answer: Vectors: Dot product a · b = |a||b| cosθ (scalar; zero if perpendicular); Cross product a × b = |a||b| sinθ n̂ (vector; magnitude gives area of parallelogram). In 3D geometry, direction cosines satisfy l² + m² + n² = 1. Shortest distance between two skew lines r = a₁ + λb₁ and r = a₂ + μb₂ is d = |(a₂ - a₁) · (b₁ × b₂)| / |b₁ × b₂|.
highlights: Vector triple product: a × (b × c) = (a · c)b - (a · b)c
Scalar triple product: [a b c] = a · (b × c) represents volume of parallelepiped
Equation of line passing through (x₁,y₁,z₁) with direction ratios (a,b,c): (x-x₁)/a = (y-y₁)/b = (z-z₁)/c
Angle between two lines with direction ratios a₁,b₁,c₁ and a₂,b₂,c₂: cosθ = (a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ + c₁c₂) / (√(Σa₁²) √(Σa₂²))

title: Maxwell's Four Equations of Electromagnetism
answer: James Clerk Maxwell unified electricity and magnetism into 4 fundamental differential/integral equations: (1) Gauss's Law for Electricity: ∮ E·dA = q/ε₀, (2) Gauss's Law for Magnetism: ∮ B·dA = 0 (no magnetic monopoles exist), (3) Faraday's Law: ∮ E·dl = -dΦ_B/dt, (4) Ampère-Maxwell Law with Displacement Current (I_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt): ∮ B·dl = μ₀(I_c + ε₀ dΦ_E/dt).
highlights: Predicted existence of Electromagnetic Waves propagating at speed of light: c = 1 / √(μ₀ε₀) ≈ 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s
Displacement Current (I_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt) resolved Ampère's law contradiction during capacitor charging
EM waves are transverse waves with E and B oscillating perpendicular to each other and to the direction of propagation (S = (1/μ₀) E × B Poynting Vector)
Heinrich Hertz experimentally verified EM waves in 1887; J.C. Bose generated millimeter microwaves in Kolkata in 1895

title: Wave Optics — Huygens' Principle, Interference & Diffraction
answer: Huygens' Principle states that every point on a wavefront acts as a secondary source of spherical wavelets spreading in all directions at the wave speed. Young's Double Slit Experiment (YDSE) demonstrates wave interference: Fringe width β = λD / d. Single-slit diffraction produces a central maximum of angular width 2λ/a.
highlights: YDSE Fringe Width: β = λD/d (where λ=wavelength, D=screen distance, d=slit separation; bright and dark fringes have equal width)
YDSE Constructive Interference (Bright): Path difference Δx = nλ (n = 0, 1, 2...); Destructive (Dark): Δx = (2n-1)λ/2
Single-slit Diffraction Minima condition: a sinθ = nλ; Central maximum width = 2λD/a (twice the width of secondary maxima)
Brewster's Law (Polarization by Reflection): tan(i_p) = μ (reflected ray is 100% plane-polarized and perpendicular to refracted ray)

title: Thermodynamics — Carnot Engine Efficiency & Second Law
answer: The Carnot Cycle is an idealized reversible thermodynamic cycle operating between two temperatures (Hot source T_H and Cold sink T_C). Carnot Efficiency: η = 1 - (T_C / T_H) = (T_H - T_C) / T_H (using absolute temperatures in Kelvin). Carnot's Theorem proves that no heat engine operating between two given temperatures can be more efficient than a Carnot engine.
highlights: Carnot Cycle 4 Steps: (1) Isothermal Expansion at T_H, (2) Reversible Adiabatic Expansion, (3) Isothermal Compression at T_C, (4) Reversible Adiabatic Compression
Carnot Efficiency η depends strictly on source and sink temperatures: η = 1 - T_C/T_H < 100% (100% efficiency requires T_C = 0 K / Absolute Zero)
Kelvin-Planck Statement: It is impossible to construct a heat engine that absorbs heat and converts 100% of it into work with no other effect
Clausius Statement: Heat cannot spontaneously flow from a cooler body to a warmer body without external work input
Entropy (S): Measure of molecular disorder; for any spontaneous irreversible process, universe entropy increases: ΔS_universe > 0

title: Nuclear Physics — Binding Energy Curve, Fission & Fusion
answer: Nuclear binding energy is the energy required to disassemble a nucleus into constituent protons and neutrons, calculated from mass defect Δm via Einstein's mass-energy equation: E = Δm · c² (where 1 amu = 931.5 MeV). Binding Energy per Nucleon (BE/A) peaks at Iron-56 (Fe-56, ~8.75 MeV/nucleon), making it the most stable nucleus. Nuclear Fission (splitting heavy nuclei like U-235) and Nuclear Fusion (merging light nuclei like H-2 + H-3 → He-4 + n + 17.6 MeV in the Sun) both release immense energy by moving toward the Fe-56 stability peak.
highlights: Mass Defect: Δm = [Z·m_p + (A-Z)·m_n] - M_nucleus; Binding Energy BE = Δm · 931.5 MeV
Nuclear Fission of Uranium-235: ²³⁵U + n → ¹⁴⁴Ba + ⁸⁹Kr + 3n + ~200 MeV energy (multiplies exponentially in uncontrolled chain reaction)
Controlled Fission in Nuclear Reactors: Control rods (Cadmium/Boron absorb neutrons) and Moderator (Heavy water D₂O / Graphite slows neutrons to thermal speeds)
Nuclear Fusion in Stars: Proton-Proton chain and CNO cycle fuse hydrogen into helium at core temperatures > 15 million K
